title: A Messenger the Cell Can Only Move

scenes.tts: Every other second messenger you have met is built, and then broken. One enzyme makes cyclic A M P, and another enzyme destroys it. Calcium is an element. No enzyme can make it, and none can break it down. So how can a bare ion carry a message?
scenes.caption: Every other second messenger you have met is built, and then broken. One enzyme makes cyclic AMP, and another enzyme destroys it. Calcium is an element. No enzyme can make it, and none can break it down. So how can a bare ion carry a message?
scenes.visual: Left column: an enzyme makes a cyclic AMP chip, a second enzyme destroys it (it fades to a dashed ghost). Right column: a calcium chip between two dashed enzyme boxes, each struck out in red; an arrow runs to a dashed box marked with a question mark: the message.
scenes.narration: Every other second messenger you have met is built, and then broken. One enzyme makes cyclic AMP, and another enzyme destroys it. Calcium is an element. No enzyme can make it, and none can break it down. So how can a bare ion carry a message?

scenes.tts: The cell moves calcium out, and keeps it out. A resting cell holds free calcium in its cytosol, the main fluid, near one hundred nanomolar. Outside, the level is one to two millimolar, ten thousand to twenty thousand times higher. The endoplasmic reticulum is a folded compartment that serves as the calcium store. There the free level is several hundred micromolar.

scenes.visual: The cell fills the frame: membrane across the top, the outside above it, the cytosol below, an ER compartment at the bottom right. Calcium dots stream out across the membrane. A level gauge shows the cytosol low; a dense crowd of dots fills the outside; a few dots sit in the cytosol; the ER holds a medium crowd.

scenes.tts: Think of a dam. The reservoir is held high at a steady cost, and opening one gate gives a flood at once. To send a calcium signal, the cell makes nothing. It opens a channel, and ions already pressed against the far side come through within milliseconds. The starting level is so low that a modest number of ions raises it tenfold, to about one micromolar.

scenes.visual: The same cell. A piece of the membrane is the gate. A crossed-out 'new calcium' box shows the cell makes nothing. The gate swings open and calcium from the outside crowd pours through into the cytosol; the gauge climbs tenfold, from 100 nM to 1 micromolar.

scenes.tts: Every channel has a pump against it. A channel only opens a path, and the gradient does the work. When it closes, a pump spends energy to take calcium out of the cytosol, and that ends the signal. The pump called Serka moves two calcium ions into the store for each A T P. Buffer proteins bind calcium and take it out of play.

scenes.visual: The gate is open and the cytosol is full. A red pump appears in the ER membrane. The gate closes; ATP chips dock on the pump and calcium dots go into the ER in pairs, two for each ATP; the gauge falls. Red buffer blobs capture the rest, the dots turning grey inside them, and the gauge returns to the resting level.

scenes.tts: A protein senses calcium with a pocket lined with oxygens. Calmodulin is a small protein with four of these pockets, called E F hands, two in each of two lobes. When calcium binds, the lobes open, then close around a helix on a target, like two hands gripping a rope. In the enzyme Cam kinase two, a segment lies across the active site and blocks it. Calmodulin grips beside that segment and pulls it clear.
scenes.caption: A protein senses calcium with a pocket lined with oxygens. Calmodulin is a small protein with four of these pockets, called EF hands, two in each of two lobes. When calcium binds, the lobes open, then close around a helix on a target, like two hands gripping a rope. In the enzyme CaM kinase II, a segment lies across the active site and blocks it. Calmodulin grips beside that segment and pulls it clear.
scenes.visual: One empty pocket takes a calcium ion. Calmodulin forms around it: two blue lobes with two pockets each. Four calcium ions fill the pockets, the lobes open into claws and close like two hands on a rope that belongs to a kinase. A red segment of that rope lies across the kinase's active site; the grip pulls the rope and the red segment slides clear, and the site turns green.

scenes.tts: A rise in an ion has become a phosphate on a protein. The cell made nothing to start it. Cyclic A M P is made and then broken. A channel lets calcium in, and a pump takes it out again. So keep this rule: calcium cannot be made or destroyed, so the cell moves it.

scenes.visual: A substrate takes a phosphate in the freed active site. The picture clears and the opening comparison returns: cyclic AMP is made by one enzyme and broken by another; calcium comes in through a channel and goes out through a pump. Under calcium, 'made' and 'destroyed' are struck out and 'moved' lights green.
